changes.claim: Why a lead in AI should translate into a hold on physical inputs has a basis in economic theory. As AI comes to substitute for human labour, the share of income paid as wages rises and a decreasing share of the returns goes to the owners of AI systems and capital, and where growth speeds up enough, an early lead can grow ever larger rather than shrink, letting a single actor outgrow the rest.

Or it might build up gradually, largely through economic processes and well before any such event: the "gradual disempowerment" described by Kulveit et al., in which the piece-by-piece replacement of human labour and judgement by AI deepens society's dependence on human participation, together with the related weakening of the incentives linking states and firms to their populations noted by Drago and Laine .

The two assumptions that drive the race — that the technology gives a decisive advantage, and that states put survival first — also make great-power conflict more likely: a power that expects to lose may strike first rather than accept a rival's permanent dominance. On their account the race is better understood as a trust dilemma than a prisoner's dilemma — so the powers can in principle cooperate to control it, and are better off doing so. Others propose explicit management regimes: Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang combine deterrence — a posture of "mutual assured AI malfunction," in which no bid for unilateral dominance invites pre-emptive sabotage — with nonproliferation and competitiveness, while RAND examines measures intended to stabilise the competition.

This scarcity is already visible in the build-out now under way: the International Energy Agency projects data-centre electricity demand falling by 2030, with the power grid itself the binding constraint, while Sevilla et al. find that power, and then chip-manufacturing capacity, are the limits most likely to bind first. How large these effects will be is contested — Acemoglu, for one, expects a far smaller impact over the coming decade — which is why, as stated at the outset, the analysis addresses the transformative case rather than predicting it will occur.

A near-term version of the same objection deserves direct attention: cheap, abundant robots. If machines can build machines, physical capacity might cease to be scarce — every usable site could be developed and no land left unclaimed — and the premise of this report would fail. The objection turns on *speed*. Robot production is indeed scaling quickly, with industry roadmaps and analysts pointing to fleets in the low millions of humanoid units per year around 2030 and unit costs falling sharply. But physical scaling is far slower than the digital progress driving it: each robot must be built from real components in real factories. Epoch AI judges that 1.5–3 million humanoids per year is clearly achievable by 2030 and 5–10 million plausible, but that current output faces no cap near 500,000 from bottlenecks such as high-precision reducers, and that reaching ten million units a year would require on the order of twenty Tesla-Gigafactory-scale plants, each taking from several months to over two years to build; the physical and production bottlenecks identified by Erdil and Besiroglu apply throughout.

Why map this at all, given how much about the future is unknowable? What follows the concentration of control — and any subsequent recursive self-improvement — cannot be foreseen: humanity may keep control or lose it, and the outcome may be benign or catastrophic. The value of the question asked here does not depend on settling that. If the long-run outcome is favourable — a world of material abundance in which people are free to live well — it matters greatly how many people survive to reach it, rather than arriving only after a large share of the world's population has perished in the economic and social dislocation that preceded it. Even under deep uncertainty about the destination, the transition itself must be survived; identifying where people might endure it is the purpose of the refuge map. The challenges of that transition, and the case for deferring them, rather than preparing for them now, to some later and wiser hand, are set out by MacAskill and Moorhouse.

If machines can build machines, physical capacity might cease to be scarce — every usable site could be developed and no land left unclaimed — and the premise of this report would fail. The objection turns on *speed*. Robot production is indeed scaling quickly, with industry roadmaps and analysts pointing to fleets in the low millions of humanoid units per year around 2030 and unit costs falling sharply. But physical scaling is far slower than the digital progress driving it: each robot must be built from real components in real factories. Epoch AI judges that 1.5–3 million humanoids per year is clearly achievable by 2030 and 5–10 million plausible, but that current output is capped near 500,000 by bottlenecks such as high-precision reducers, and that reaching ten million units a year would require on the order of twenty Tesla-Gigafactory-scale plants, each taking from several months to over two years to build; the physical and production bottlenecks identified by Erdil and Besiroglu apply throughout.

Selective access and abrupt withdrawal were thus both on display: access can be granted along national lines and revoked overnight, without consultation and with no process by which an allied government can contest it. The European Commission took the episode as proof of "why Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty" .

Such concentration could arrive by either of two routes. It might come suddenly, through recursive self-improvement — an AI system improving its own capabilities in an accelerating cycle, the "intelligence explosion" first described by Good.

The two assumptions that drive the race — that the technology gives a decisive advantage, and that states put survival first — also make great-power conflict more likely: a power that expects to lose may strike first rather than accept a rival's permanent dominance. On their account the race is better understood as a trust dilemma than a prisoner's dilemma — so the powers can in principle cooperate to control it, and are better off doing so. Others propose explicit management regimes: Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang combine deterrence — a posture of "mutual assured AI malfunction," in which any bid for unilateral dominance invites pre-emptive sabotage — with nonproliferation and competitiveness, while RAND examines measures intended to stabilise the competition.
